Declare the trait `excludes { Number }`, or make it exclude arrays, `excludes { HasRank }`. Or declare the `+` in an object, not in a trait: an object excludes every trait that it does not extend, because no other type can extend it. Otherwise walk refuses the program at load: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker refuses such a pair in one component, but accepts it against the library's `+` (row 918). Give a trait with its own functional `-`, `MIN` or `MAX` the same fix: the library declares these in the same form.
25	
26	## Traits and objects
27	
28	**The compiled checker applies the exclusion rule (P-43, P-97).** It refuses a type that extends two instantiations of one generic trait. Walk does not apply the rule: it runs such a type, and refuses overloads on two instantiations, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])`, because it does not read them as excluding (row 416). The specification marks the Working Draft's examples that break the rule "Not allowed": do not copy them.
29	
30	**A `comprises` clause speaks of values (P-60).** Every value of the trait that declares it is a value of a listed type. So a generic trait need not be listed if every type below it is below a listed type, as `Integral[\I\]` below `AnyIntegral`. A Java `permits` list names each direct subtype; this clause need not. Read so, several declarations can together cover the meet of two overloads. At load, walk checks extenders only against the clauses of the program's main component (row 551).
31	
32	**`override` widens.** An `override` overrides an inherited declaration only where the inherited parameter types are strictly narrower than its own. To replace an inherited declaration at its own parameter types, declare it again without `override`. An `override` in a trait also overrides in every type below it. The checker checks that an overriding return type is a subtype. Walk refuses at load an `override` that, by this rule, overrides nothing, so a Java-style `override` in the library stops every program. Two departures: the checker accepts such an `override` (row 653), and the code generator refuses every `override` modifier (row 650).
33	
34	**An object defines an inherited abstract method by bodies that together cover its parameter types (P-147).** It needs one body at those types, or several narrower bodies that cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk refuses at load an object without static parameters that leaves one uncovered. Walk skips this check for a generic object (row 665). Walk stops its search for a cover at limits that `interpreter.md` gives, and the checker at the same limits. The checker refuses a cover by several bodies where the abstract or a covering method has static parameters (row 725).
35	
36	**In a self-typed trait the checker types `self` as the trait met with the implementing type.** A trait `T` is self-typed if both conditions hold:
37	
38	- `T` has no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`;
39	- `T` has a parameter `X` bounded by `T` itself, as `trait T[\X extends T[\X\]\]` (P-146), or by a self-typed trait `U[\X\]` that `T` extends, as `trait T[\X extends U[\X\]\] extends U[\X\]`.
40	
41	In `T`'s bodies, `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X`. So `floor(self): I = self` in `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]` is valid without a cast. The checker refuses a type that extends `T[\A\]` and is not an `A`. A compiled body of `T` that returns `self` fails the JVM's verification when its class loads (row 695).
42	
43	When the checker applies the overloading rules to a method of `T`, `self` has the type `T[\X\]`, except in its test of whether two domains exclude each other. There `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X` (P-157). With this reading and the bounds that the test reads ("Dispatch and overloading"), the library's generic `+` and `-` between an array and a number are valid beside `AdditiveGroup`'s own. Walk reads `self` in the same way, so it loads such a pair in the library and in a program's own component. Walk's load check, which is not the verdict ("Dispatch and overloading"), still refuses the pair in two cases:
44	
45	- `T` is self-typed only through another self-typed trait that it extends;
46	- `T`'s method has static parameters of its own.
47	
48	**An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (P-156).** An indexed type is a type whose values `a[i]` subscripts, such as an array. Its index parameter is the static parameter that gives the type of `i`. In the library, and in your own generic over such a type, write `I extends Index`. Walk runs the code without the bound. The checker refuses it when it checks against the interpreter's library, as the count stage does (`compiler.md`). Of the integer types, only `ZZ32` extends `Index`, and `Range` excludes `Index`. To the checker a numeral is an `IntLiteral`, which is no `Index`. So it refuses `f(3)` for `f(x: Index)`. Walk takes it (row 364). Pass a `ZZ32` value there instead. `a[3]` stays valid, because an array indexed by `ZZ32` takes a `ZZ32`. The Working Draft lets no trait type hold a tuple, but here a tuple whose element types are all `Index` types is an `Index`. So `m[i, j]` passes the pair `(i, j)` as one index. `Index` extends only `Any`, so such a tuple is still no `Object`. The empty tuple `()` is no `Index`. A function over `Index` and one over a tuple of `Index` types do not exclude each other. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares no `Index`, so a program that names it does not compile: write the bound only in code that runs under walk or is checked against the interpreter's library. Two departures:
49	
50	- the checker refuses a tuple expression at a parameter of type `Index`, but takes one at a parameter of type `I`, where `I extends Index` (row 805);
51	- walk loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it (row 806).
52	
53	**Pairs and triples are ordered only where each element type extends `StandardPartialOrder`.** This holds for `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `CMP`. Walk refuses another element type at the call, also where earlier elements decide, as `(1,()) < (2,())`. It also refuses numbers of two run-time types at one position, as `(1,2) < (1,2.5)` (row 511). Unordered deciding elements give `false`, or `Unordered` for `CMP`. The checker orders a `List[\E\]` only where `E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\]`, so a list of `RR64` has no order there (P-154). Walk orders every list (row 774). A list's `=` stays element by element.
54	
55	**Where a type declares no `=`, `=` is strict equivalence, `SEQV` (P-168).** Strict equivalence is the operator `≣` (STRICTLY EQUIVALENT TO), written `SEQV` or `===` in ASCII. The operator `≡` (IDENTICAL TO, `EQV` or `EQUIV`) is a different one: logical equivalence on booleans. The interpreter's library declares it for no type, and walk stops on it (row 184): write `a <-> b`. The library's `=` over `Any` answers `a SEQV b`. `SEQV` follows the specification on both paths:
56	
57	- values of different types are never equivalent;
58	- a value object is equivalent field by field, a tuple element by element, an integer, a character or a boolean by its value, and a float by its bits;
59	- a reference object, a string among them, is equivalent only to itself;
60	- a function is equivalent to itself, but may be found unequal to another that behaves the same.
61	
62	So for a value object `V` without its own `=`, `V(s) = V(t)` is `false` where `s` and `t` are equal strings made by two computations. Under walk, each evaluation of a string literal makes a new string, unlike Java, which interns literals. So `"ab" SEQV "ab"` and `V("ab") = V("ab")` are `false`. The library declares `=` on pairs and triples only, so `(s, 1, 2, 3) = (t, 1, 2, 3)` is `false` too. Both `false` answers are the rule's: assert them as correct. Under walk a float numeral is a `FloatLiteral`, a type of its own, so it is not equivalent to a computed `RR64` (`interpreter.md`, "How walk evaluates a program"). To compare by content, give the value object an `=`, or compare the parts. A string's `=` compares text. Under walk, `≠` (`=/=` or `NE`) and `assert(x, y, msg)` reach a type's own `=` only if the type extends a library trait that declares `=`, such as `Equality` (row 807). Otherwise write `assert(x = y, msg)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library declares no `=` over `Any` and none on tuples. Its own `≣`, declared as `===`, compares strings and `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `RR32` and `RR64` by `=`, not by bits or identity (row 908).
63	
64	## Static parameters, `where` clauses and sizes
65	
66	**A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound, not Scala's `Nothing` (P-48).** The checker takes the intersection of its upper bounds, narrowed by the expected type. Under walk, a parameter whose bound names itself stays open, printed `OPEN`, as in `BoxU[\OPEN\]`. Every value passes `OPEN` itself. Where walk compares overloads, a type that holds `OPEN` admits only what it admits at `Bottom`: beside `pick(x: Any)`, `pick(x: (T,T))` takes no `(1, 2)`. Walk still gives `Bottom` to these parameters:
67	
68	- one with two bounds, neither below the other (row 591);
69	- one that an argument bounds only from above, with a bound that names another static parameter (row 612);
70	- one that only the result of a function expression without a return type fixes (row 587).
71	
72	**Only the checker gives a call written as an argument the enclosing call's context (P-51).** If the enclosing call fails as written, the checker types the inner call again against each declaration's parameter type. So `takesBox64(mk())` compiles for `mk[\T\](): BoxT[\T\]`. Walk gives an argument no expected type, so there `mk()` takes its bound (row 705). Under walk, write `mk[\ZZ64\]()`.
73	
74	**Three `where` forms are built (P-151).** Conditional extension is an `extends` entry with a `where` clause that binds no variable and states only constraints `T extends SomeTrait`. The type extends the parent only where they hold, as `List[\E\]` extends `LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] }`. The other two forms:
75	
76	- a condition of a function or method on its own static parameters, or of a method on its trait's, checked at a call;
77	- a type variable of a `where` clause in a `comprises` clause, as `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`.
78	
79	The checker reads an `extends` entry with any other `where` clause as unconditional, without a message. Walk and the compiled runtime apply a conditional extension at every instance (row 774). Walk runs a dotted call that breaks a method's condition (row 777). The code generator accepts a declaration's own `where` clause but emits no code for it, so the compiled runtime does not check it. A compiled call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, dies at run time (row 867). `compiler.md` gives the checker's gaps.
80	
81	**Sizes are compared by their written form (P-55).** The checker checks sizes against their kind, and the runtime carries each as a descriptor. Two sizes are equal when they are written alike after numeral arithmetic: `2 3` is `6`, but `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`. A static parameter is not known to differ from a numeral, so in `typecase N[\b0\] of N[\0\] => ...` the arm is reachable. The checker refuses a size power above the exponent 4096, except of 0, 1 or -1. Walk refuses a negative exponent. The class loader computes a size without checking its kind, and stops on a negative exponent with a Java exception (row 675).
82	
83	**A size known only at run time comes from `reflect` in `NatReflect.fsi`.** Its value, a `NatParam`, passed where the object type `N[\n\]` is expected, binds `n` at the call. Such a call does not run compiled yet. Until the switch-over, compiled programs do not link `NatReflect`, which is part of the interpreter's library. After the switch-over, such a call still fails, for a second reason. `NatParam` is declared `comprises { N[\n\] } where [\nat n\]`, so its `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause size. A compiled call fails the JVM's verification if it passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected (row 307). This holds for a program's own trait too.
84	
85	## Numbers
86	
87	**The number types are flat siblings (P-43).** The record calls this choice route A. Route C is the way not chosen: a checker rule under which the number types could nest again. The record still calls the number and order traits "the tower". That word does not mean that they nest.
88	
89	**Under walk a numeral has a run-time class.** The checker types an integer numeral as `IntLiteral`, a sibling under `Number` that converts to the integer types, `QQ` and `RR64` (P-76). Walk gives a numeral the class `Int`, `Long` or `BigNum` by its value. These classes stand for `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` and `ZZ`, but a generic instantiates at the class. Walk prints these classes as `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` and `ZZ`, also inside static arguments, so a printed type does not show the instance: `Cell(3)` prints `Cell[\ZZ32\]` but is a `Cell[\Int\]`, and no `Cell[\ZZ32\]` (row 364). Where you need a `Cell[\ZZ32\]`, write `Cell[\ZZ32\](3)`. Walk's own error messages say `Int`. Walk answers `IntLiteral`'s arithmetic as a `ZZ32` (row 578). The library's factories `array1` and `array2` give a `Vector` or `Matrix` only at the eight number types, not at a user subtype of `Number`. Elsewhere they give a plain array, whose `+` and unary `-` fail dispatch under walk. Under walk, an inferred element type is a run-time class, so they give a plain array (row 721). Write the static argument.
90	
91	**Arguments convert by declared coercions, and a generic call promotes.** Walk converts at a call, a typed binding and an assignment, and chooses the coercion by the run-time value; the checker chooses it statically (P-59). Promotion instantiates a generic declaration at the narrowest type into which all its arguments coerce (P-74). So `f[\T\](a: T, b: T)` on a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` runs at `ZZ64`. Walk does not promote the elements of a tuple or varargs: it takes their join (rows 395, 511). Where several declarations apply only by coercion and none is more specific, both paths stop: "Ambiguous coercion". Where the tied declarations differ only at the positions of the call's numerals, the checker reads the numeral as `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where the value does not fit.
92	
93	**An integer converts to another integer type by a checked getter or by a low-bits function (P-161).** To convert a value, write a getter: `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` or `asZZ`. It keeps the value or raises `IntegerOverflow`. The functions `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big` keep the low bits and never raise, as Java's `(int)` does. So `narrow` of a `ZZ64` outside `ZZ32`'s range wraps silently. Under walk, each fixed-width type has all five, and one that keeps the type returns the value, as `widen` of a `ZZ64`. Of the five, `ZZ` has only `big`, so `narrow(z)` finds no declaration: write `z.asZZ32`. A fixed-width type's `bitsAs…` getter gives its bits at the other sign, as `bitsAsNN32` of a `ZZ32`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude has 8 of the 25 getters, `ZZ64`'s `asZZ32` among them, none on `ZZ`, and no `big`. Of the low-bits functions it has only those that change the type, as `narrow` of a `ZZ64` (row 349).
94	
95	**`Number` declares nothing (P-165).** Each of the eight number types, and `IntLiteral`, declares its own `asFloat` into `RR64`. So generic code over `T extends Number` can call on a `T` no method or operator that the number types declare, `asFloat` among them. Two numbers of different types compare by `=` only where a coercion carries one into the other: the library declares `=` for each such pair, so a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` of equal value are `=`. Otherwise `=` is `SEQV` ("Traits and objects"), and answers `false` without an error: `1/2 = 0.5` is `false`, as is a `ZZ64` against an equal `RR64`. To compare values across types at known types, write `asFloat(x) = y`. In generic code over `T extends Number`, declare your function once for each number type instead. A program may also declare its own number type below `Number` (P-160).
96	
97	**An integer power answers its base's type (P-153).** In the interpreter's library, `^` takes an exponent of any integer type. At a negative exponent, 1 and -1 give their power, 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and other bases raise `IntegerOverflow`. For a result that is not an integer, write `2.0^(-1)`, or a `QQ` base as `(2/3)^(-1)`, not `10^(-k)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has integer powers only at `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64`, each with an exponent of its own type; its `RR64` power takes an `RR64` or a `ZZ32` exponent, a negative one included. Its `ZZ32` power gives 0 at a negative exponent for other bases. At a base of 0 it throws a Java exception that no `catch` sees (rows 441, 523).
98	
99	**`/` on two integers answers a `QQ`.** So `7 / 2` is `7/2`, not 3. Truncate with `DIV`, on both paths. `DIV` answers its operands' type and rounds toward zero. For a float, make one operand a float, as `(1.0 s) / n` for `ZZ32` values `s` and `n`. Convert each `ZZ64` operand with `asFloat`, as `asFloat(s) / asFloat(n)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has no `QQ` and declares `/` only at `RR64`, so a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error.
100	
101	## Reductions and comprehensions
102	
103	A clause form is a reduction or comprehension with generators in brackets, as `SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)`.
104	
105	**A reduction's static argument depends on the path.** The checker does not infer it for `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`, whose bound names the parameter (row 731). Write it in every clause form, as `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. Other reductions take their bound, or the expected type where the bound does not fit. Walk instantiates a reduction at its value's declared type: a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's return type, also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a field, a top-level variable, a parameter and an assignment do not direct it. Else walk takes the join of the elements' run-time types. If that join is outside the reduction's bound, each `+` runs at its operands' types. An element that does not convert to the instance stops in `__bigOperator`, "body param 1". Departures under walk:
106	
107	- with no declared type, an empty `SUM` gives the integer 0 (row 716);
108	- a comprehension inside another clause form is built at its elements' run-time types (rows 20, 717);
109	- a written static argument that is not a number type ends an empty `SUM` in `CastError` (row 436).
110	
111	**A reduction without an identity lifts its elements to `Maybe[\R\]` inside the reduction.** `BIG MIN`, `BIG MAX` and the string reduction `BIG //` extend `AssociativeReduction[\R\]`, whose `simpleJoin` takes and answers `R`. `BIG MAX` over a generator still answers `R`. Walk refuses at load a reduction without static parameters that declares `simpleJoin` at `Any` or untyped. A generic one stops at its first join. The team's tests declare `simpleJoin` so: do not copy them.
112	
113	## Implementation limits
114	
115	**Walk has no static types.** Walk will run the checker only after the switch-over (P-12). So walk runs programs that the checker refuses. Besides a `Boolean`, it takes a `Maybe` as an `if` condition, `Just` as true and `Nothing` as false. It refuses any other value. The specification and the checker take only a `Boolean`, so do not write a `Maybe` condition. The compiled path's own limits are in `compiler.md`.
116	
117	**Write every parameter type.** The compiled path refuses a parameter without a type, of a function, a method or a local function: "Missing parameter type for". Walk runs it, except in a method that implements an abstract one (row 405). A component's function that leaves out its return type takes the api's declaration at its parameter types. With none or several, the checker types the body.
118

# Quiz grading 1

Cases graded: 4 (6, 16, 17, 30). Right: 3 (16, 17, 30). Right without its path or scope qualification: 1 (case 6). Wrong: 0.

The case 6 partial counts against the orientation. No passage misled the reader. A rule that the key needs for the compiled half is missing from the core, the area parts and the orientation: that the compiler's prelude declares `narrow` on `ZZ64` and `widen` on `ZZ32`, and that its `narrow` keeps the low bits (row 346). The fix is one clause in the orientation's P-161 rule, given under case 6. The same clause would also settle the lookups that the reader left open in cases 17 and 30.

## Case 6: arithmetic that must wrap

**Grade: right without its scope qualification (the compiled half).**

What matches the key:

- The walk spelling is the key's: `h := (31 DOTTIMES h) DOTPLUS c`, with the inner product parenthesised. The key's outer pair adds nothing: the expression is the whole right-hand side of `:=`.
- The plain port `31 h + c` raises `IntegerOverflow` under walk, and the reader says so.
- The reader also gives the second spelling right, `h := narrow(31 widen(h) + widen(c))`. It says the `ZZ64` step cannot overflow, and that `narrow` keeps the low 32 bits without raising.
- After the switch-over, the compiled path takes the interpreter's library, which declares the operators.
- The loop over the characters is made sequential with `seq(...)`. The key does not ask for this, but it is right (core, "Parallelism and mutable state").
- None of the key's Wrong answers appears: no plain `31 h + c` expected to wrap, no `MOD 2^32`, and no `.asZZ32` on the `ZZ64` step.

What is missing:

- On the compiled path before the switch-over, the reader gives no wrapping spelling. It says the passages are silent, and plans to grep the three prelude files and `ledger-find:` for `DOTPLUS` and `DOTTIMES`.
- Its plan handles only "the prelude declares neither operator": the line is a static error, and a compiled test of it is an `XXX` test.
- It says nothing about the result that the key names: the prelude declares `DOTPLUS` but saturates with it, and its `BOXPLUS` wraps (row 348). The prelude has no `DOTTIMES`.
- It does not carry its own `narrow` spelling over to the compiled path. The key accepts that spelling on both paths, before and after the switch-over (row 346; `CompilerBuiltin.fsi:206`, `:269`).

The key's **Partial** covers this: "a reader who says that no product wraps compiled until the switch-over has missed the `narrow` spelling". The reader does not say that no spelling wraps, but its compiled answer gets no further than its chosen line being refused.

**Cause: a rule that the key needs is missing.**

- The orientation's P-161 rule, which the reader quotes, ends: "Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude has 8 of the 25 getters, none on `ZZ`, and no `big` (row 349)."
- That sentence says nothing of the prelude's `narrow` and `widen`. The reader read it as silent on them, and said so in case 30.
- The prelude's reversed `DOTPLUS` and `BOXPLUS` (row 348) are in no part either. `library.md`'s wrapping bullet gives the interpreter library's spelling only.

Fix in the orientation, P-161's last sentence, about this length:

"Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude has 8 of the 25 getters, `ZZ64`'s `asZZ32` among them, none on `ZZ`, and no `big` (row 349). Its `narrow` of a `ZZ64` and `widen` of a `ZZ32` keep the low bits, as here (row 346)."

With that, a reader writes the `narrow` spelling for both paths, which the key accepts as a full answer. Row 348 could go in `library.md`'s wrapping bullet as well, but the case does not need it.

## Case 16: a numeral at an `NN32` binding

**Grade: right.**

- Under walk the binding is refused, because walk's numeral is an `Int` (a `ZZ32`) (row 454). The reader writes `n: NN32 = unsigned(3)`, the form in `tests-writing.md`.
- On the compiled path `n: NN32 = 3` works: the checker types the numeral `IntLiteral`, which converts to the integer types (P-76).
- Both paths are answered, and neither of the key's Wrong answers appears. The getter `(3).asNN32` is not used, so the malformed `3.asNN32` cannot come up.
- The extras are sound:
  - walk's refusal is a departure, not to be asserted as correct;
  - before using `unsigned` in a compiled test, the reader greps the prelude for it and reads row 349. The prelude declares it on `ZZ32` (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:270`), and the key measures that `unsigned(3)` compiles and gives 3.

## Case 17: a loop over `ZZ64` bounds whose steps depend on each other

**Grade: right.**

- The loop is over a `ZZ32` range, `seq(lo32 # count)`. The reason is the key's: a range over `ZZ64` is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one (`library.md`, the ranges bullet).
- The bounds are converted with the checked getter, `lo.asZZ32` and `(hi - lo).asZZ32`, which raises `IntegerOverflow` where a value does not fit. So the key's trap, `narrow` taken as the exact conversion, does not reach the reader. Because the count is converted by the getter, an out-of-range `hi - lo` raises rather than silently running no step.
- Each element is widened, `j.asZZ64`. The reader notes that the declared coercion would also convert `j`. The key's own example uses that coercion.
- The loop is sequential, for the key's reason: each step needs the total before it, and `total :=` in a parallel `for` is a race. The reader also notes that `atomic` would not fix the order.
- The `if lo < hi` guard is unneeded, since `lo.asZZ32 # n` with `n` at or below 0 runs no step (the key's measured `3 # 0` and `3 # (-1)`). It is harmless. The reader says the parts do not state what such a range does, and that is so.
- Compiled path, which the key says is not needed for a right answer: the reader names its lookups (row 349 for the 8 getters, a grep of the prelude for `seq`) and what it does with each result. The plan holds up. The prelude's `ZZ32` has no `asZZ64` (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:212-213`), and the reader's fallback, drop it and let the coercion convert `j`, is the right one. `ZZ64`'s `asZZ32` (`:150`) and `seq` (`CompilerLibrary.fsi:113`) are declared.

## Case 30: an exact integer conversion, and one that keeps the low bits

**Grade: right.**

- (a) `toInt(n: ZZ64): ZZ32 = n.asZZ32`. At 2^31 it raises `IntegerOverflow`, which a `catch` sees, as Java's `toIntExact` throws.
- (b) `toInt(n: ZZ): ZZ32 = n.asZZ32`. At 2^31 it raises `IntegerOverflow`. The reader rules out `narrow` on the `ZZ`, for the key's reason: under walk it finds no declaration, and `ZZ`'s only low-bits function is `big`.
- (c) `fold(h: ZZ64): ZZ32 = narrow(h)`. It keeps the low 32 bits and never raises: 7 at 2^32 + 7, as Java's `(int)` gives.
- None of the key's Wrong answers appears: no `narrow` in (a) or (b), no `narrow(n.asZZ64)`, no `h.asZZ32` or mask in (c).
- The extras are right:
  - the inputs are built from numerals, not as `2^31`, which raises because the base is a `ZZ32` (P-153, P-73);
  - the two `toInt` overloads are declared one per sibling type.
- Compiled path today:
  - (b) does not compile, because the prelude has no getter on `ZZ`. This is the key's answer (row 349).
  - (a) and (c) are left to a lookup that names its sources: row 349 and a grep of `CompilerBuiltin.fsi` and `CompilerLibrary.fsi` for `asZZ32` and `narrow`. It also says what follows when one is missing (no compile until the switch-over, nothing added to the prelude, an `XXX` compile test). Both are declared (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:150`, `:206`), so the lookup reaches the key's answer: (a) and (c) compile.
  - The question asks only whether they compile, so the key's point that they also give the same values is not required.
  - After the switch-over all three compile (P-37).
- The lookup was needed only because the orientation's prelude sentence does not name `ZZ64`'s `asZZ32` among the 8 or mention the prelude's `narrow`. The fix proposed under case 6 settles this too.

Cases graded: 4 (6, 16, 17, 30). Right: 4. Right without its path or scope qualification: 0. Wrong: 0.

No case counts against the orientation. The fix round's new sentence in the P-161 rule worked. Round 1's case 6 partial came from that sentence being missing. Reader 2 quotes the new sentence, "Of the low-bits functions it has only those that change the type, as `narrow` of a `ZZ64` (row 349)", and from it writes the `narrow` spelling for the compiled path. In cases 17 and 30 the reader quotes "`ZZ64`'s `asZZ32` among them", so the lookups that reader 1 left open in those cases are settled. Three points below are not counted, because no case turns on them. They are for the writer.

## Case 6: arithmetic that must wrap

**Grade: right.**

- Walk spelling: `h := (31 DOTTIMES h) DOTPLUS c`, with the inner product in parentheses. This is the key's spelling. The key's outer pair adds nothing, because the expression is the whole right-hand side of `:=`.
- The plain `31 h + c` raises `IntegerOverflow` under walk, and the reader says so.
- Compiled path, before the switch-over: the reader writes the low-bits form, `w: ZZ64 = h; h := narrow(31 w + c)`, and says it runs under walk too. This is the key's second spelling. The key writes `widen(h)` and `widen(c)`. The reader instead uses the declared coercion from `ZZ32` into `ZZ64`, at the binding and at `+`. That is P-74's rule for mixed widths ("Mixed integer widths convert by declared coercions"). The prelude declares that coercion (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:149`), so the spelling holds on both paths. The reader states why the step is exact in `ZZ64`, and that `narrow` keeps the low 32 bits as Java's `(int)` does.
- So the answer gives "the `narrow` spelling for both", which the key's **Scope** accepts as a full answer. After the switch-over the operators' line holds on both paths, and the reader says so.
- The loop is made sequential with `seq(...)`, for the right reason. The key does not ask for this.
- None of the key's Wrong answers appears: no plain form expected to wrap, no `MOD 2^32`, and no `.asZZ32` on the `ZZ64` step.

Not counted: the reader's lookup for `DOTPLUS` and `DOTTIMES` in the prelude says "If the prelude has the operators, the same line works there". The prelude declares a `DOTPLUS` that saturates, and its `BOXPLUS` wraps (row 348). It declares no `DOTTIMES`. So the lookup still lands on the reader's "does not" branch and the `narrow` form. The answer stands. But a port of a sum alone would find `DOTPLUS` and take it for wrapping. Row 348 is still in no part. Round 1 made the same point, and this case does not need it.

## Case 16: a numeral at an `NN32` binding

**Grade: right.**

- Walk: the binding is refused, because walk's numeral is an `Int` (row 454). The reader writes `n: NN32 = unsigned(3)`, the form `tests-writing.md` gives. It names `asNN32` as the checked form for a computed value, and does not write the malformed `3.asNN32`.
- Compiled: the reader says `n: NN32 = 3` is accepted, since the checker types the numeral `IntLiteral` (P-76). It plans to confirm this with a `fortress compile`. That is the key's answer.
- The reader names `unsigned(3)` as the spelling for both paths, and plans to grep the prelude for it. The prelude declares it on `ZZ32` (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:270`), and the key measures that it compiles and gives 3.
- Neither of the key's Wrong answers appears.
- An extra, not in the key, holds up by the orientation's P-165 rule and case 26's key: under walk, `assert(n, 3, "n")` compares an `NN32` with a `ZZ32`, and no coercion joins those two types. Walk's two-value `assert` compares by `=/=` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:307-308`). So `=` falls to `SEQV` and the assert fails. The reader instead writes `assert(n = unsigned(3), "n")`. This was not measured.

## Case 17: a loop over `ZZ64` bounds whose steps depend on each other

**Grade: right.**

- The loop is over a `ZZ32` range, `seq(lo32 # (hi32 - lo32))`. The reason is the key's: a range over `ZZ64` is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one.
- The bounds are converted with the checked getter `asZZ32`, so the key's trap, `narrow` taken as the exact conversion, does not reach the reader. The count `hi32 - lo32` is a plain `ZZ32` subtraction. Where it leaves `ZZ32`, it raises `IntegerOverflow` (P-73). It does not silently run no step, so it meets the key's concern as `(hi - lo).asZZ32` does.
- Each element is widened, `i.asZZ64`. The reader notes that the declared coercion would also do it, which is the key's own example.
- The loop is sequential, for the key's reason: each step needs the total before it, and `total :=` in a parallel `for` is a race.
- The reader looks up what `#` does with a count at or below 0, with a guard as fallback. This is not needed, since such a range runs no step (the key's measured `3 # 0` and `3 # (-1)`). It is harmless.
- Compiled path, which the key does not require: the reader checks the prelude for `seq` and for `ZZ32`'s `asZZ64`, and says what it does if either is missing. `seq` is declared (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi:113`). `ZZ32`'s `asZZ64` is not (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:210-213`). The reader's fallback for that result, passing `i` and letting the coercion widen it, is right.

## Case 30: an exact integer conversion, and one that keeps the low bits

**Grade: right.**

- (a) `n.asZZ32` on a `ZZ64`. At 2^31 it raises `IntegerOverflow`, in the role of Java's `ArithmeticException`. The reader rules out `narrow` because it wraps silently.
- (b) `n.asZZ32` on a `ZZ`. At 2^31 it raises. The reader rules out `narrow(n)` because `ZZ` has only `big`.
- (c) `narrow(h)` on a `ZZ64`. It gives 7 at 2^32 + 7 and never raises.
- None of the key's Wrong answers appears.
- The inputs are bound from numerals at the wide types, not written `2^31` (P-153).
- Compiled path today: (a) and (c) compile, and (b) is a static error until the switch-over, because the prelude has no getter on `ZZ`. That is the key's **Scope**. After the switch-over all three compile. The reader also plans to confirm in a compiled test that the prelude's `asZZ32` raises at 2^31. The key measured that it does.
- The reader names (b) `toIntBig` and does not overload `toInt`. The key overloads it. This does not change the conversions, so it is not graded.

Not counted: the reason that the reader gives for the rename is doubtful. It says that a `ZZ32` or numeral argument would fit `toInt(ZZ64)` and `toInt(ZZ)` "only by coercion, with neither more specific", so the call would be "Ambiguous coercion" on both paths. It also says that it does not know whether `ZZ64` and `ZZ` exclude each other.

- They do: `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:635`.
- The specification's Coercion Resolution makes `ZZ64` more specific than `ZZ`: `ZZ64` excludes `ZZ`, coerces to it, and rejects it, because every type that coerces into `ZZ64` excludes `ZZ` (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:502-540`). The chapter's printed example has this same shape, `f(ZZ64)` beside `f(ZZ128)` on a `ZZ32` argument (`:579-620`).
- So the pair is a valid overloading, and the call is not a tie. This was not measured on either path.

The reader took "siblings" to mean "neither more specific". The orientation's sentence "Where several declarations apply only by coercion and none is more specific" does not say that a coercion between excluding siblings can make one of them more specific. No case of the quiz turns on this yet.

- P-161 **The integer conversions: checked `as…` getters that raise `IntegerOverflow` on every integer type, `bitsAs…` getters for the bit pattern, today's names as the low-bits forms, and `ZZ`'s `narrow` and `widen` deleted.** On each of `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64` and `ZZ`, the getters `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` and `asZZ` raise `IntegerOverflow` where the value does not fit: of the 25, 5 are identities, 7 equal the coercions and 13 can raise. The four fixed widths have the compiler prelude's `bitsAs…` getters. `narrow`, `widen`, `unsigned`, `signed` and `big` keep the low bits, each declared on every type where it applies, so that no call reaches one through a coercion. `ZZ`'s conversions out are its five getters; the callers of its `narrow` and `widen` (`Library/Format.fss`, `Library/QuickCheck.fss`, the demo `sudoku.fss`, the test `XXXZZNarrowRungP`) move onto `.asZZ32` or `.asZZ64` with their values unchanged. P-72 (`narrow` keeps the low 32 bits on the fixed widths), P-73 (fixed-width arithmetic raises) and P-74 (an exact conversion is implicit) stand. So `z.asZZ64` raises for a `ZZ` too large, and `unsigned` of a negative value keeps the low bits, with `x.asNN32` or `x.asNN64` as its check. Why: the team's later work, Steele's prelude, made `asZZ32` raise in 2011 and named the bits `bitsAs…` in 2012; the specification's general sentence says that an integer result that overflows throws `IntegerOverflow`; a plain name that checks beside a name that tells its loss is Swift's and Julia's pattern; and `ZZ`'s two are wrong code: its `widen` can narrow, and turns 2^63 negative.

\subsection{Object Trait Types}
\seclabel{object-traits}

An object trait type is a trait type defined by an object declaration.
Object declarations do not include \KWD{excludes} clauses,
but an object trait type cannot be extended.
Thus, an object trait type excludes any type that is not its supertype.

**The rule against its sources.** I checked each sentence of line 93 against the record and the tree:

- `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big` keep the low bits and never raise (P-161, F-331, F-132).
- "Under walk, each fixed-width type has all five, and one that keeps the type returns the value, as `widen` of a `ZZ64`." Each of the four fixed widths declares all five (`FortressLibrary.fsi:553-557`, `:626-631`, `:702-706`; `FortressBuiltin.fsi:188-193`). F-331: "on a value that already has its result type, as `widen` of a `ZZ64`, each returns the value".
- "Of the five, `ZZ` has only `big`, so `narrow(z)` finds no declaration." This holds under walk (`FortressLibrary.fsi:772`; F-331). It holds compiled too: the prelude's `ZZ` declares no conversion out, and no coercion leads out of `ZZ` (`CompilerBuiltin.fsi:103-145`; row 349). So the fix round was right to drop "under walk" (`cold-read.md` item 2.12).
- The `bitsAs…` getters give the bits at the other sign. Each fixed width has one, on both paths (`FortressLibrary.fsi:505`, `:573`, `:649`; `FortressBuiltin.fsi:140`; `CompilerBuiltin.fsi:152`, `:214`, `:277`, `:337`). So the rule rightly gives them no path qualifier.
- "Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude has 8 of the 25 getters, `ZZ64`'s `asZZ32` among them, none on `ZZ`, and no `big`." This matches row 349's list of the 8 and `CompilerBuiltin.fsi:150`.
- "Of the low-bits functions it has only those that change the type, as `narrow` of a `ZZ64` (row 349)." The prelude declares exactly eight: `narrow` and `unsigned` on `ZZ64`, `widen` and `unsigned` on `ZZ32`, `widen` and `signed` on `NN32`, `narrow` and `signed` on `NN64`. Each changes the type, and they are every type-changing low-bits function except `big`, which the sentence before excludes. Row 349 says the same: "no `narrow`, `widen`, `signed` or `unsigned` that returns its argument".
  - The sentence says nothing of a call that reaches a wider type's function by coercion. Row 349's notes: "`narrow` of a `ZZ32` 43 compiles by coercion through `ZZ64`'s `coerce(x: ZZ32)` ... and gives 43". A reader of the sentence expects such a call to be refused. It compiles and gives the same value, so no value is wrong.

**The checks.**
- **Preservation.** Both failures are fixed in the final text. Failure 1, the compiled half of row 349, is fixed by "Under walk" and the new sentence on the prelude's low-bits functions. Failure 2, the wrap example, is fixed by "outside `ZZ32`'s range". No sentence says more than its source.

The fix round wrote that rule from the prelude's declarations and row 349. It did not cite row 346, which is closed, and it gave its reason (writer 2's log). Round 2: four of four right. Reader 2 quotes the new sentence in cases 6, 17 and 30.

On `ZZ` I would write `z.asZZ32`. In compiled code, I would check which of the 8 getters the prelude has." Its points on line 93 do not send a worker wrong:
  - **Item 2.13** (40%) asks whether "all five" means the getters. Read either way, the sentence is true: under walk each fixed width has all five getters too. "Under walk" is narrower than it need be, since the checker reads the same library, but no action changes.
  - **Item 2.1** (70%, over several passages) notes that the second limit sentence continues an "Until the switch-over" sentence without opening with it. Its subject, "it", is the prelude that the sentence before names. Its row, 349, "Closes at the switch-over (P-37)". The two markers lead to one action: do not fix it in the prelude, and do not assert it as correct in a test. The batch 27 judge read line 62's `===` sentence the same way. Item 2.2 is the same convention, and it is listed below.
  - **Section 3** calls "8 of the 25 getters, `ZZ64`'s `asZZ32` among them" a partial count. It is not wrong. The clause on `ZZ64`'s `asZZ32` settled the lookups that reader 1 left open in cases 17 and 30 (`quiz-grade-2.md`), so it earns its place.

Cases 17 and 30, which test each mistake, were right in both rounds.
